intro: Daniel 9:24-27 is the most precise time prophecy in the Bible: seventy weeks, or sevens, decreed for Daniel's people and his holy city. How you count them shapes how you read the rest of Bible prophecy. This study walks through the text phrase by phrase, lets you run the count yourself, compares the four main ways of reading it, and then lays every major end-time passage on one timeline from Daniel's exile to the fall of Jerusalem. It follows the partial preterist reading: the seventy weeks reach their goal in Christ's first coming, and the desolation they announce fell in AD 70. The other views, their strongest points, and the objections to this reading are all set out fairly.
orthodoxy: Every Christian view in this study holds that Daniel is true prophecy and that Christ will return bodily to raise the dead and judge the world. Partial preterism sees most of the prophecies about the end of the old covenant age fulfilled by AD 70, while Christ's second coming, the resurrection and the final judgement remain future, as the creeds confess. Full preterism, which places the resurrection and the return in the past, is outside the historic creeds and is not the view taught here.

goals.kept: Israel's rebellion came to its full measure when its leaders rejected and killed the Messiah.

goals.goal: To put an end to sin
goals.kept: Christ appeared once at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but for the whole world.
The righteousness of God has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ.

goals.goal: To seal up vision and prophet
goals.kept: The Law and the Prophets were until John; Christ is the fulfilment the prophets looked for.

goals.goal: To anoint a most holy place
goals.kept: Jesus was anointed with the Holy Spirit at his baptism, and entered the true holy place with his own blood.

phrases.fulfilled: Seventy sevens of years, 490 years, as one unbroken block, answering Daniel's prayer about Jeremiah's seventy years (9:2).
phrases.futurist: Seventy sevens, but with the clock stopped after the sixty-ninth; the last seven is still future.

phrases.phrase: about your people and your holy city
phrases.fulfilled: The period concerns Israel and Jerusalem up to the coming of the Messiah and the end of the old covenant order.
phrases.futurist: The whole prophecy concerns national Israel, so the church age is not counted.

phrases.phrase: to finish the transgression ... to anoint a most holy place
phrases.fulfilled: All six goals are accomplished by Christ's death, resurrection and anointing (see the checklist).
phrases.futurist: Several goals, such as everlasting righteousness, wait for Israel's national repentance at the second coming.

phrases.phrase: from the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem
phrases.fulfilled: Usually the decree of Artaxerxes to Ezra in 457 BC, which gave authority to restore the city's life and law.
phrases.futurist: Usually Artaxerxes' commission to Nehemiah in 444 BC, which explicitly concerned rebuilding the walls.

phrases.phrase: to the coming of an anointed one, a prince, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks
phrases.fulfilled: Sixty-nine weeks, 483 years, from 457 BC reach AD 27, when Jesus was anointed with the Spirit at his baptism.
phrases.futurist: 483 years of 360 days from 444 BC reach the triumphal entry in AD 33.

phrases.phrase: after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing
phrases.fulfilled: The crucifixion, in the middle of the seventieth week, about three and a half years after the baptism.
phrases.futurist: The crucifixion, after which the prophetic clock stops.

phrases.phrase: the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary
phrases.fulfilled: The Roman armies under Titus destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70.
phrases.futurist: The Romans destroyed the city, and their future ruler, the Antichrist, is the prince who is to come.

phrases.phrase: its end shall come with a flood, and to the end there shall be war
phrases.fulfilled: The Jewish war of AD 66-70, which ended in overwhelming desolation.
phrases.futurist: War and desolation continue through history until the end.

phrases.phrase: he shall make a strong covenant with many for one week
phrases.fulfilled: The Messiah confirms the covenant with many: the new covenant in his blood, poured out for many (Matthew 26:28).
phrases.futurist: The Antichrist makes a seven-year treaty with Israel.

phrases.phrase: for half of the week he shall put an end to sacrifice and offering
phrases.fulfilled: By his death the Messiah ended the meaning of the temple sacrifices; the veil was torn (Hebrews 10:11-18).
phrases.futurist: The Antichrist stops the sacrifices in a rebuilt temple halfway through the tribulation.

phrases.phrase: on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate
phrases.fulfilled: The abomination of desolation Jesus warned of (Matthew 24:15), the armies surrounding Jerusalem (Luke 21:20).
phrases.futurist: The Antichrist's image or presence in a future temple.

phrases.phrase: until the decreed end is poured out on the desolator
phrases.fulfilled: The judgement on Jerusalem was poured out, and later the desolating power itself was judged.
phrases.futurist: The Antichrist is destroyed at Christ's return.

decrees.note: Cyrus allows the exiles to return and rebuild the temple. Isaiah 44:28 says he will say of Jerusalem, “she shall be built.”
Darius confirms Cyrus' decree and the temple is finished in 516 BC.
Authority to restore worship, appoint judges and enforce the law in Judea; Ezra 9:9 speaks of a wall in Judah and Jerusalem.
Permission to rebuild the walls and gates of Jerusalem, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes.

models.name: Messianic, continuous (partial preterist and many Reformed)
models.sixtyNine: AD 27: Jesus anointed at his baptism
models.seventieth: AD 27-34: the cross in the middle (AD 30/31), then the gospel to Samaria and the Gentiles; the desolation follows in AD 70
models.prince: The Messiah confirms the covenant; the Roman people of the coming prince destroy the city
models.strength: Counts the weeks without a break and finds the Messiah at the centre, as Daniel 9:24-26 does.
models.weakness: The end of the seventieth week is not marked by a single dramatic event, and dating Jesus' ministry has a margin of a year or two.

models.name: Dispensational, with a gap
models.sixtyNine: AD 33: the triumphal entry, using 360-day years
models.seventieth: Still future: a seven-year tribulation after the rapture
models.prince: The Antichrist makes a seven-year treaty with Israel and breaks it
models.strength: Takes “the prince who is to come” as the subject of 9:27 and links the abomination with 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 13.
models.weakness: Inserts a gap of nearly two thousand years that the text does not mention, and needs 360-day years and a rebuilt temple.

models.name: Critical (Maccabean)
models.sixtyNine: 171 BC: the murder of the high priest Onias III
models.seventieth: 171-164 BC: Antiochus IV desecrates the temple
models.strength: Matches Daniel 8 and 11, which clearly describe Antiochus.
models.weakness: 587 to 164 BC is about 423 years, not 490, so it must say the writer miscounted; and Jesus treats Daniel 9's abomination as still future in his day.
models.from: 587 BC, Jeremiah's word at the fall of Jerusalem

models.name: Symbolic
models.sixtyNine: The first coming of Christ, in round numbers
models.seventieth: The whole church age, to the second coming
models.prince: Often the Antichrist at the end of the age
models.strength: Respects the symbolic use of seven and ten in apocalyptic writing.
models.weakness: Loses the precision of 7 + 62 + 1 weeks that the text itself gives, and makes the last week thousands of years long.

timeline.label: Daniel taken to Babylon
timeline.text: Nebuchadnezzar's first siege; Daniel among the young exiles.

timeline.label: The statue dream
timeline.text: Four kingdoms, then a stone that becomes a mountain: God's kingdom set up in the days of those kings.

timeline.label: Jerusalem and the temple destroyed
timeline.text: The first destruction; the seventy years of Jeremiah run their course.

timeline.label: Daniel's prayer; Gabriel's answer
timeline.text: In the first year of Darius the Mede, Daniel reads Jeremiah and prays; Gabriel announces seventy weeks.

timeline.label: Cyrus' decree
timeline.text: The exiles may return and rebuild the temple.

timeline.label: Second temple finished
timeline.text: Under Darius I, the temple is completed.

timeline.label: Decree to Ezra: the count begins
timeline.text: Artaxerxes authorises Ezra to restore the law and life of Jerusalem. Start of the seventy weeks on the messianic count.

timeline.label: Nehemiah rebuilds the walls
timeline.text: The walls are built “in a troubled time” (Daniel 9:25). The dispensational start of the count.

timeline.label: End of the first seven weeks
timeline.text: Forty-nine years from 457 BC: the restored city and the close of the Old Testament period.

timeline.label: Alexander conquers Persia
timeline.text: The goat of Daniel 8 breaks the ram's two horns.

timeline.label: Antiochus defiles the temple
timeline.text: The little horn of Daniel 8 and the king of Daniel 11 set up an abomination; the Maccabees resist.

timeline.label: The temple rededicated
timeline.text: Hanukkah; Daniel 8's 2,300 evenings and mornings are completed.

timeline.label: Rome takes Jerusalem
timeline.text: Pompey enters the temple; the fourth kingdom rules Judea.

timeline.label: Jesus anointed at his baptism
timeline.text: Sixty-nine weeks from 457 BC: the Anointed One appears. “The time is fulfilled.”

timeline.label: The Messiah cut off
timeline.text: In the middle of the seventieth week, Jesus is crucified; the temple veil is torn.

timeline.label: Pentecost and the new covenant
timeline.text: The Spirit is poured out; Joel's prophecy is fulfilled; the covenant is confirmed with many in Jerusalem.

timeline.label: End of the seventieth week
timeline.text: About seven years after the baptism: Stephen martyred, the gospel goes to Samaria and soon to Gentiles, and Paul is called.

timeline.label: Famine under Claudius
timeline.text: The famine Agabus foretold.

timeline.label: The gospel in all the world
timeline.text: Paul writes that the gospel has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven.

timeline.label: Nero's persecution
timeline.text: After the fire of Rome, Christians are tortured and killed; Peter and Paul die in these years.

timeline.label: The Jewish revolt; Cestius withdraws
timeline.text: Roman armies surround Jerusalem, then withdraw. Christians, remembering Jesus' warning, flee.

timeline.label: Vespasian invades Galilee
timeline.text: The war spreads through the land; false prophets and zealots multiply.

timeline.label: Year of the four emperors
timeline.text: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian: civil war shakes Rome.

timeline.label: Jerusalem and the temple destroyed
timeline.text: Titus' armies burn the temple; not one stone is left on another. The people of the prince destroy the city and sanctuary.

timeline.label: Masada falls
timeline.text: The last stronghold of the revolt is taken.

passages.title: The statue and the stone
passages.timeText: In the days of those kings
passages.when: Christ's first coming, in the Roman era
passages.reading: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome; God's kingdom set up in Rome's days and growing to fill the earth.
passages.futurist: A revived Roman empire of ten kings in the future, destroyed at the second coming.

passages.title: The Son of Man and the four beasts
passages.timeText: The time came when the saints possessed the kingdom
passages.reading: The Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive the kingdom: the ascension (Acts 1-2). The little horn persecutes the saints.
passages.futurist: The little horn is the future Antichrist, and the kingdom begins at the second coming.

passages.title: Ram, goat and little horn
passages.timeText: The time of the end; 2,300 evenings and mornings
passages.reading: Persia, Alexander and Antiochus IV, who desecrated the temple; the sanctuary restored in 164 BC.
passages.futurist: Antiochus, and also a pattern of the future Antichrist.

passages.title: Seventy weeks
passages.timeText: Seventy weeks are decreed
passages.when: 457 BC to AD 34, with the desolation in AD 70
passages.reading: The Messiah anointed, cut off in mid-week, confirming the covenant; the city destroyed by the people of the coming prince.
passages.futurist: The seventieth week is a future seven-year tribulation.

passages.title: Kings of the north and south
passages.timeText: At the time of the end
passages.when: Persia to the Herods and Rome
passages.reading: A detailed history of the Ptolemies and Seleucids; verses 36-45 are read as Herod or Rome, or still as Antiochus.
passages.futurist: From verse 36 on, the future Antichrist.

passages.title: Great distress and resurrection
passages.timeText: When the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end
passages.when: AD 70, with the final resurrection still ahead
passages.reading: The great distress is the fall of Jerusalem (12:7); the resurrection language includes the final resurrection, which Jesus also affirms (John 5:28-29).
passages.futurist: The tribulation and resurrection at the end of history.

passages.title: The Spirit poured out
passages.timeText: Before the great and awesome day of the LORD
passages.reading: Peter: “this is what was spoken.” The day of the Lord on Jerusalem followed within that generation.
passages.futurist: Pentecost was partial; the cosmic signs are future.

passages.title: The day of the LORD on Jerusalem
passages.timeText: A day is coming for the LORD
passages.reading: Nations gathered against Jerusalem, half the city exiled; living waters flow out (John 7:38); the LORD king over all the earth.
passages.futurist: A literal future battle at Jerusalem, with Christ's feet splitting the Mount of Olives.

passages.title: Elijah before the day
passages.timeText: Before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes
passages.reading: Jesus says John is the Elijah to come (Matthew 11:14); the day burned like an oven on that generation.
passages.futurist: Elijah may still come before the second coming.

passages.title: The Olivet Discourse
passages.timeText: This generation will not pass away
passages.reading: The temple's destruction and its signs, all within Jesus' generation.
passages.futurist: Signs of the end of history and the second coming.

passages.title: That day and hour
passages.timeText: Concerning that day and hour no one knows
passages.when: Many see a shift to the final coming here
passages.reading: Many partial preterists see the final return and judgement from 24:36 or 25:31; others place more of it in AD 70.
passages.futurist: The second coming and final judgement.

passages.title: Some standing here
passages.timeText: Some standing here will not taste death
passages.reading: The Son of Man coming in his kingdom: the transfiguration, resurrection, Pentecost and judgement on Jerusalem.
passages.futurist: Fulfilled in the transfiguration as a preview.

passages.title: Jerusalem surrounded by armies
passages.timeText: Its desolation has come near
passages.reading: Rome's armies surround the city; the people are killed or led captive.
passages.futurist: Mostly agreed as AD 70, with the end of the times of the Gentiles still future.

passages.title: The man of lawlessness
passages.timeText: The mystery of lawlessness is already at work
passages.reading: A rebel who exalts himself in the temple that still stood; the restrainer known to the readers.
passages.futurist: The future Antichrist in a rebuilt temple.

passages.title: The dead in Christ rise
passages.timeText: The Lord himself will descend
passages.reading: Christ's bodily return and the resurrection of believers: still future.
passages.futurist: Future; dispensationalists see a pre-tribulation rapture here.

passages.title: The resurrection and the end
passages.timeText: Then comes the end
passages.reading: Christ reigns until death, the last enemy, is destroyed at the resurrection: still future.
passages.futurist: Future.

passages.title: This same Jesus will come
passages.timeText: In the same way
passages.reading: Jesus will return bodily and visibly, as he ascended.
passages.futurist: Future.

passages.title: The day of the Lord as a thief
passages.timeText: In the last days scoffers will come
passages.reading: Some read the passing of heaven and earth as the end of the old covenant world; many partial preterists read it as the final judgement.
passages.futurist: The final dissolution and renewal of creation.

passages.title: The six seals
passages.timeText: Things that must soon take place
passages.reading: Conquest, war, famine and death on the land, culminating in the great day of wrath on Jerusalem.
passages.futurist: The first half of the future tribulation.

passages.title: The temple measured; two witnesses
passages.timeText: Forty-two months
passages.reading: The temple still stands to be measured; the holy city trampled for forty-two months.
passages.futurist: A future temple and two future prophets.

passages.title: The beast and its number
passages.timeText: Forty-two months
passages.reading: The beast's number, 666, fits Nero Caesar in Hebrew letters; his persecution lasted about forty-two months.
passages.futurist: The future Antichrist and his mark.

passages.title: The harlot and seven kings
passages.timeText: Five have fallen, one is
passages.reading: Seven hills and seven kings of Rome; the sixth reigning as John writes. Many read the harlot as apostate Jerusalem.
passages.futurist: A future world religious and political system.

passages.title: The thousand years and the last judgement
passages.timeText: A thousand years
passages.when: The gospel age to the final judgement
passages.reading: Christ's present reign with his saints; the final judgement and resurrection are still future (20:11-15).
passages.futurist: A future earthly thousand-year kingdom after the return.

passages.title: New heavens and new earth
passages.timeText: Behold, I am making all things new
passages.when: Begun in Christ, complete at the end
passages.reading: The new covenant world begun in the church and consummated at the final renewal.
passages.futurist: The eternal state after the millennium.

fallacies.name: The inserted gap
fallacies.problem: Daniel gives a single block: seventy weeks, divided 7 + 62 + 1. Placing nearly two thousand years between the 69th and 70th weeks adds something the text never mentions; no reader before the 19th century counted it that way as a system.
fallacies.reply: Count the weeks continuously and the Messiah appears at the 69th and is cut off in the 70th, as the text says.

fallacies.name: The wrong “he”
fallacies.problem: In 9:26 “the prince who is to come” is not the subject; “the people” are. The person the whole passage is about is the Anointed One. Making “he” in 9:27 a future Antichrist skips the Messiah to reach a minor noun.
fallacies.reply: The Messiah confirms the covenant with many, as Jesus said of his blood “poured out for many.”

fallacies.name: A covenant turned into a treaty
fallacies.problem: Nothing in the text speaks of a peace treaty or of breaking one. The word is covenant, and the verb means to make strong or confirm.
fallacies.reply: In Daniel 9, covenant is God's covenant (9:4). The Messiah confirms it.

fallacies.name: Special pleading on the year
fallacies.problem: The 360-day “prophetic year” is used only when it makes the count fit 444 BC to AD 33. Israel's calendar added months to keep pace with the sun, so its years averaged 365 days.
fallacies.reply: A normal year count from 457 BC reaches AD 27 without adjustment.

fallacies.name: Elastic “generation”
fallacies.problem: “This generation” is read literally in Matthew 23:36 (judgement on Jesus' hearers) but as “this race” or “the future generation” in 24:34, eleven verses later.
fallacies.reply: Read the same phrase the same way in both places.

fallacies.name: Elastic “soon”
fallacies.problem: Revelation says its events “must soon take place” and “the time is near,” while Daniel was told to seal his book because the time was far off. Reading “near” as two thousand years reverses the contrast.
fallacies.reply: Daniel's distant visions became near in John's day.

fallacies.name: Unfalsifiable double fulfilment
fallacies.problem: When a sign fits the first century, it is called a partial fulfilment with a greater one still to come. That makes any prophecy endlessly postponable and impossible to test.
fallacies.reply: Look for a fulfilment the New Testament itself names before adding a second one.

fallacies.name: Newspaper exegesis
fallacies.problem: Reading today's news into the text, a form of the presentism fallacy, has produced failed predictions in every generation since the second century.
fallacies.reply: Begin with what the text meant to its first hearers.

fallacies.name: A temple the text does not mention
fallacies.problem: Daniel 9 mentions only the temple that would be destroyed (9:26), which was the second temple. A third temple must be supplied from elsewhere.
fallacies.reply: The sanctuary of Daniel 9 is the one Titus burned.

fallacies.name: A seven-year tribulation built from one verse
fallacies.problem: The seven-year tribulation rests on putting the 70th week in the future. Revelation never mentions a seven-year period, and no text places a rapture before it.
fallacies.reply: Revelation's numbers are 42 months, 1,260 days and “a time, times and half a time”: half of a week, not a whole one.

fallacies.name: The miscounted prophecy
fallacies.problem: Dating the seventy weeks from 587 to 164 BC gives about 423 years, so the critical view must say the author got his own number wrong.
fallacies.reply: A count that reaches the Messiah exactly is a better explanation than an author who miscounted.

fallacies.name: Ruling out prophecy in advance
fallacies.problem: The late dating of Daniel often begins from the assumption that detailed prediction is impossible. That decides the question before the evidence is weighed.
fallacies.reply: Jesus calls Daniel a prophet and treats his abomination as still future in AD 30.

fallacies.name: Precision dissolved
fallacies.problem: The text divides the weeks into 7, 62 and 1 and places events after the 62. A purely symbolic count cannot explain why such divisions are given.
fallacies.reply: The divisions mark real stages: rebuilding, waiting, and the Messiah's week.

fallacies.name: Everything already past
fallacies.problem: Full preterism places the resurrection and Christ's return in AD 70, but Paul condemns those who say the resurrection has already happened.
fallacies.reply: Partial preterism keeps the bodily return and resurrection future.

strawmen.strawman: Preterists say Jesus already came back and there is no future resurrection.
strawmen.whyFalse: That is full preterism, which partial preterists reject.
strawmen.accurate: Partial preterists hold that the judgement on Jerusalem was a coming of Christ in judgement, and that his bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgement are still future.

strawmen.whyFalse: Eusebius (c. 325) applied Matthew 24 to AD 70 at length, as did Chrysostom.
strawmen.accurate: Many early writers read the Olivet Discourse as fulfilled in AD 70; the systematic preterist commentary on Revelation dates from Luis de Alcazar (1614).

strawmen.whyFalse: They believe it was fulfilled exactly, on time.
strawmen.accurate: Preterists see the fulfilment of Daniel 9 and Matthew 24 as one of the strongest proofs that Scripture is true.

strawmen.whyFalse: They take the time words literally and read symbols as apocalyptic language, as the prophets used it.
strawmen.accurate: They read “soon,” “near” and “this generation” plainly, and the cosmic imagery as the prophets' language for the fall of nations (Isaiah 13:10).

strawmen.strawman: Dispensationalists teach two ways of salvation.
strawmen.whyFalse: Some early notes were read that way, but dispensationalists teach salvation by grace through faith in every age.
strawmen.accurate: They distinguish God's programs for Israel and the church, not ways of being saved.

strawmen.strawman: Dispensationalists want war in the Middle East.
strawmen.whyFalse: Expecting a war is not wanting one.
strawmen.accurate: Most believe Scripture predicts future conflict and pray for peace and for Israel's salvation.

strawmen.strawman: Anyone who dates Daniel late is an unbeliever.
strawmen.whyFalse: Some believing scholars read Daniel as apocalyptic literature written in the Maccabean crisis.
strawmen.accurate: The critical view rests on literary and historical arguments, which should be answered on their merits.

strawmen.whyFalse: Many Reformers were historicists and read Revelation as a survey of church history.
strawmen.accurate: Historicism reads Daniel and Revelation as a map of history from the apostles to the end, and was the main Protestant view for three centuries.

strawmen.whyFalse: Most accept that Daniel 8 and 11 describe Antiochus and that AD 70 fulfilled part of the Olivet Discourse.
strawmen.accurate: Futurists see near and far fulfilments, with the decisive one still ahead.

objections.q: Doesn't Isaiah 61, quoted in Luke 4, show prophecies can have gaps?
objections.a: Jesus stops reading before “the day of vengeance.” But Isaiah 61 has no numbered count; Daniel 9 counts seventy weeks and says what happens after the 62nd. A pause in reading is not a gap in a count. And the day of vengeance came within that generation (Luke 21:22).

objections.q: If the seventieth week ended about AD 34, why was the city destroyed in AD 70?
objections.a: Daniel 9:26 places the destruction “after the sixty-two weeks” without saying it falls inside the seventy. The seventy weeks decree the Messiah's work; the desolation is its consequence, “determined” for the people who rejected him. Jesus gave that generation forty years to repent.

objections.q: Isn't “the prince who is to come” the nearest antecedent for “he” in 9:27?
objections.a: Grammatically, “prince” is in a dependent phrase (“the people of the prince”). The main figure of the passage is the Anointed One. Many Hebrew scholars, ancient and modern, take the Messiah as the subject of 9:27, and the covenant language fits him.

objections.q: Didn't Jesus say the abomination of desolation was still future?
objections.a: Yes, future in AD 30, and he told his hearers to flee when they saw it. Luke explains it as Jerusalem surrounded by armies. It came in AD 66-70.

objections.q: Why did Jesus not say the time was 457 BC plus 490 years?
objections.a: He announced it: “the time is fulfilled” (Mark 1:15). Luke reports that the people were in expectation of the Messiah in John's day (Luke 3:15), and Jewish writers of the period expected a deliverer around then.

objections.q: Is the date of Jesus' baptism certain enough?
objections.a: Luke dates John's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, which most place in AD 28-29, with some counting from his co-regency in AD 26-27. Jesus was about thirty. The fit is within a year or two, remarkable for a prophecy given five centuries earlier.

objections.q: Doesn't 2 Thessalonians 2 require a future temple?
objections.a: When Paul wrote, around AD 51, the temple stood, and he said the lawlessness was already at work and the readers knew the restrainer. A first-century fulfilment fits his words.

objections.q: Why does Revelation say “a thousand years” if it is symbolic?
objections.a: Revelation is a book of signs (1:1). Its numbers are symbolic throughout: seven spirits, 144,000, twelve gates. A thousand years pictures a long, complete reign. Partial preterists still expect a future final judgement after it.

objections.q: Was the gospel really preached to the whole world before AD 70?
objections.a: Paul says so: it was proclaimed in all creation under heaven and bearing fruit in the whole world. The word for world in Matthew 24:14 is the inhabited earth, the Roman world, as in Luke 2:1.

objections.q: Doesn't Zechariah 14 describe a future battle?
objections.a: Its picture of nations gathered against Jerusalem and half the city exiled fits AD 70, and its living waters and the LORD as king over all the earth are applied to the gospel age (John 7:38). Some partial preterists also see final elements in it.

objections.q: Isn't preterism just a way to avoid looking for Christ's return?
objections.a: No. Partial preterists confess the bodily return and look for it. What they reject is the expectation of a seven-year tribulation, a rebuilt temple and an Antichrist treaty drawn from Daniel 9.

objections.q: If Daniel 8 is Antiochus, why not Daniel 9 as well?
objections.a: Daniel 8 is explicitly about Greece (8:21) and its numbers fit 171-164 BC. Daniel 9 is about the Anointed One being cut off and the city and sanctuary destroyed, which Antiochus did not do: he defiled the temple but did not destroy it.

questions.short: A unit of seven: here seven years. Seventy weeks are 490 years.
questions.answer: The Hebrew word means a seven. Daniel had been reading Jeremiah's seventy years of exile (9:2), and Gabriel answers with seventy sevens: seven times longer, echoing the sabbath-year laws of Leviticus 25-26, where neglected sabbath years brought exile. The exile lasted seventy years; the full restoration would take seventy weeks of years.
examples: Leviticus 25:8: seven weeks of years, forty-nine years, to the jubilee.
2 Chronicles 36:21: the land kept its sabbaths seventy years.
Daniel 10:2 adds “days” when it means weeks of days.
questions.other: Symbolic readers take the sevens as round periods rather than exact years.

questions.q: Who are “your people” and “your holy city”?
questions.short: Daniel's people, Israel, and Jerusalem. The weeks set the time left for them before the Messiah comes and the old order ends.
questions.answer: Gabriel tells Daniel the seventy weeks are decreed for Israel and Jerusalem. Within that time the Messiah would come, deal with sin and confirm the covenant; and because the city rejected him, it would be destroyed. The partial preterist reading sees the prophecy entirely kept in that history. Dispensationalists agree it concerns Israel and therefore leave the church age out of the count.
examples: Daniel 9:16-19: Daniel prays for your city and your people.
Luke 19:42-44: Jesus weeps that Jerusalem did not know the time of its visitation.
questions.other: Dispensationalists hold that because the prophecy concerns Israel, its last week must wait for God to resume his program with the nation.

questions.q: Were all six goals of Daniel 9:24 fulfilled?
questions.short: Yes. Each describes what Christ accomplished: sin ended, atonement made, everlasting righteousness brought in, prophecy sealed and the Most Holy anointed.
questions.answer: The six goals are not political; they are about sin and righteousness. The New Testament says Christ put away sin by his sacrifice once at the end of the ages, made atonement, revealed God's righteousness, and was anointed with the Spirit. The checklist on this page pairs each goal with the verse that says it was done.
examples: Hebrews 9:26: once at the end of the ages to put away sin.
Romans 3:21-25: the righteousness of God revealed; Christ the propitiation.
Acts 10:38: God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit.
questions.other: Dispensationalists say “everlasting righteousness” and the end of Israel's transgression await the nation's repentance at Christ's return.

questions.q: Who is the Anointed One who is “cut off”?
questions.short: Jesus the Messiah, crucified. Almost all Christian views agree.
questions.answer: After the sixty-two weeks an anointed one would be cut off and have nothing. The word is used of being killed (Genesis 9:11). Isaiah says the Servant was “cut off out of the land of the living” (53:8). Jesus was crucified around AD 30, about three and a half years into his ministry, in the middle of the seventieth week.
examples: Isaiah 53:8: cut off out of the land of the living.
John 2:13; 6:4; 11:55: three Passovers in John's Gospel, suggesting a ministry of over three years.
questions.other: Critical scholars identify the anointed one as the high priest Onias III, murdered in 171 BC.

questions.short: With a word to restore and build Jerusalem. The best candidates are 457 BC (Ezra) and 444 BC (Nehemiah).
questions.answer: Four decrees are proposed: Cyrus (538), Darius (520), Artaxerxes to Ezra (457) and Artaxerxes to Nehemiah (444). Cyrus' decree is about the temple. The 457 decree restored the city's legal and civic life and funded its restoration; Ezra 9:9 already speaks of a wall. The 444 commission rebuilt the walls. Try each one in the calculator on this page.
examples: Ezra 7:25-26: appoint magistrates and judges.
Ezra 9:9: to give us a wall in Judea and Jerusalem.
Nehemiah 2:5: send me to the city, that I may rebuild it.
questions.other: Dispensationalists prefer 444 BC because Nehemiah's commission explicitly concerns the city's walls.

questions.q: Should the years be 365 days or 360?
questions.short: Israel's calendar kept pace with the sun by adding a month when needed, so its years averaged about 365 days. The 360-day year is needed only for the 444 BC count.
questions.answer: Revelation equates 1,260 days with 42 months, which some take as proof of 30-day months and 360-day years. But that is a symbolic half-week, not a calendar rule. Jewish years were lunar months adjusted to the solar year by an extra month, as the festivals had to fall at harvest time. Counting normal years from 457 BC reaches AD 27.
examples: 457 BC + 483 years = AD 27 (there is no year 0).
444 BC + 483 years of 360 days (about 476 solar years) = AD 33.
questions.other: Dispensationalists argue that Genesis 7-8 (150 days for five months) shows 30-day months in prophetic reckoning.

questions.q: Why is the first period seven weeks?
questions.short: The first forty-nine years cover the rebuilding of the city “in a troubled time,” from Ezra and Nehemiah to the end of the Old Testament era.
questions.answer: Gabriel says the city would be rebuilt with squares and moat, but in a troubled time. Ezra and Nehemiah record opposition, and Malachi, the last prophet, wrote in this period. After that came sixty-two weeks of waiting with no new prophet, until John the Baptist and Jesus.
examples: Nehemiah 4:17: each worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other.
Luke 16:16: the Law and the Prophets were until John.
questions.other: Critical scholars place the seven weeks from 587 to 538 BC, ending with Cyrus.

questions.q: When did the seventieth week end?
questions.short: About AD 34, seven years after Jesus' baptism, when the gospel moved beyond Jerusalem to Samaria and the Gentiles after Stephen's death.
questions.answer: For the first years after Pentecost the apostles preached in Jerusalem, confirming the covenant with many in Israel. Then Stephen was stoned, persecution scattered the church, Philip preached in Samaria, Paul was called as apostle to the Gentiles, and Peter went to Cornelius. The week of the covenant's confirmation to Israel came to its end, and the door opened to the nations.
examples: Acts 8:1-5: scattered through Judea and Samaria.
Acts 9:15: a chosen instrument to carry my name before the Gentiles.
Acts 13:46: since you thrust it aside, we turn to the Gentiles.
questions.other: Some preterists place the last week at AD 66-73 instead, with its middle at the destruction of the temple in AD 70.

questions.q: What are the main ways of reading the seventy weeks?
questions.short: Four: the continuous messianic count (partial preterist and many Reformed), the dispensational gap, the critical Maccabean view, and the symbolic view.
questions.answer: The messianic view counts the weeks straight through to Christ. The dispensational view stops the clock after the 69th week and places the 70th in a future tribulation. The critical view reads the whole prophecy as written in the 160s BC about Antiochus IV. The symbolic view treats the weeks as an era stretching from Cyrus to the second coming. The 70-square chart on this page lets you see each one.
examples: Messianic: E. J. Young, many Reformed and partial preterist writers.
Gap: Robert Anderson, Harold Hoehner, most dispensationalists.
Critical: most modern academic commentaries.
questions.other: Each view has a best case; they are set out side by side on this page.

questions.q: Where did the gap view come from?
questions.short: Some early writers placed part of the last week near the end, but a systematic gap with a future Antichrist treaty developed with 19th-century futurism and dispensationalism.
questions.answer: Irenaeus and Hippolytus linked the Antichrist to half a week at the end, so the idea of a future half-week is old. But many early writers, including Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius and Augustine, related the weeks to Christ's first coming. The detailed gap model, with a seven-year treaty and a pre-tribulation rapture, took shape in the work of Darby, Robert Anderson's The Coming Prince (1881) and the Scofield Bible.
examples: Hippolytus, Commentary on Daniel: the last week at the end, split by the Antichrist.
Tertullian, Against the Jews 8: the weeks reach Christ and the destruction of Jerusalem.
Robert Anderson, The Coming Prince (1881): the 360-day count to AD 32.
questions.other: Dispensationalists point to Irenaeus and Hippolytus as early witnesses to a future final week.

questions.q: Why do many scholars think Daniel 9 is about Antiochus IV?
questions.short: Because Daniel 8 and 11 clearly describe Antiochus, and they date the book to his time. But Daniel 9's numbers and events fit Christ better.
questions.answer: Daniel 8 names Greece and describes a king who desecrates the temple and stops the sacrifice, which Antiochus did in 167 BC. Critical scholars read chapter 9 the same way, with the anointed one as Onias III. But Antiochus did not destroy the city and sanctuary (9:26), the count falls well short of 490 years, and Jesus treated the abomination of desolation as future in his own day.
examples: 1 Maccabees 1:54: the abomination set up on the altar in 167 BC.
Matthew 24:15: Jesus refers to Daniel's abomination as still to come.
questions.other: Critical scholars respond that apocalyptic numbers are schematic, and that Jesus reapplied Daniel's language to new events.

questions.short: He called himself the Son of Man of Daniel 7, announced that the time was fulfilled, and warned that Daniel's abomination of desolation would come on that generation.
questions.answer: Jesus' favourite title came from Daniel 7:13. At his trial he said the high priest would see the Son of Man seated at the right hand and coming with the clouds (Matthew 26:64). He told the disciples to flee Judea when they saw the abomination Daniel spoke of. Each use ties Daniel to his own ministry and that generation.
examples: Mark 1:15: the time is fulfilled.
Matthew 26:64: you will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds.
Matthew 24:15-16: let those in Judea flee.
questions.other: Futurists agree Jesus is the Son of Man, but read his coming on the clouds as the second coming.

questions.q: Is the Son of Man's coming in Daniel 7 the second coming?
questions.short: In Daniel 7 the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days, upward, to receive a kingdom. That is the ascension.
questions.answer: Daniel sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days, and given dominion, glory and a kingdom. The movement is toward God, not toward earth. Jesus ascended in a cloud and sat at God's right hand, receiving all authority (Matthew 28:18). His “coming on the clouds” in judgement on Jerusalem showed that enthronement.
examples: Acts 1:9: a cloud took him out of their sight.
Matthew 28:18: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.
Ephesians 1:20-22: seated at his right hand, far above all rule.
questions.other: Futurists read Daniel 7:13 with Revelation 1:7 as the visible second coming.

questions.q: What is still future on a partial preterist reading?
questions.short: Christ's bodily return, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgement, and the full renewal of creation.
questions.answer: Partial preterism is not the view that everything has happened. Acts 1:11 promises Jesus will come back in the same way he went. 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 describe the resurrection at his coming. Revelation 20:11-15 describes the final judgement. These remain the Christian hope. The passage map on this page marks each text as fulfilled, future, or both.
examples: Acts 1:11: this same Jesus will come in the same way.
1 Corinthians 15:23-26: the last enemy to be destroyed is death.
Revelation 20:12: the dead were judged by what they had done.
questions.other: Full preterists say even these were fulfilled in AD 70; partial preterists and every historic creed reject that.

questions.q: How do Daniel's visions fit together?
questions.short: Daniel 2 and 7 give the four kingdoms ending with Rome and God's kingdom; Daniel 8 and 11 zoom in on Greece and Antiochus; Daniel 9 sets the clock to the Messiah; Daniel 12 ends with the shattering of the holy people's power.
questions.answer: Daniel 2 and 7 run in parallel: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, and then the kingdom of God set up in Rome's days. Daniel 8 and 11 give detail on the Greek period and Antiochus' persecution. Daniel 9 gives the time to the Messiah and the destruction that follows his rejection. Daniel 12 says all these things would be finished when the power of the holy people was shattered: the end of the old covenant order in AD 70.
examples: Daniel 2:44: in the days of those kings.
Daniel 12:7: when the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end, all these things will be finished.
questions.other: Futurists see a revived Rome and the Antichrist at the end of several of these visions.

questions.q: What principles help us read time prophecies well?
questions.short: Read the time words plainly, let the New Testament interpret the Old, look first for a fulfilment the Bible itself names, and do not read the news into the text.
questions.answer: First, take time statements as their first hearers would: “near” means near. Second, follow the apostles' own interpretations of the prophets. Third, look for the fulfilment the Bible names before adding a second one. Fourth, read symbols as the prophets used them: falling stars are the fall of rulers (Isaiah 13:10). Fifth, keep the great certainties: Christ's return, resurrection and judgement.
examples: Isaiah 13:10, 19: stars darkened at the fall of Babylon.
Acts 2:16: this is what was spoken.
Revelation 22:10: do not seal up the words, for the time is near.
questions.other: Futurists add that some prophecies have near and far fulfilments, so the first-century fulfilment may not be the last.

questions.q: Why does the seventy weeks prophecy matter?
questions.short: Because it shows God fixed the time of the Messiah five centuries in advance, and because it decides whether we expect a future seven-year tribulation.
questions.answer: A prophecy that names the time of the Messiah's coming and death, and the destruction of the temple that followed, is a powerful witness to Jesus. It also governs much of modern prophecy teaching: the seven-year tribulation, the Antichrist's treaty and the rebuilt temple all depend on placing the 70th week in the future. Reading it as fulfilled keeps Christ at the centre of the prophecy.
examples: Luke 24:27: beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
Galatians 4:4: when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son.
questions.other: Dispensationalists see the prophecy as equally Christ-centred, with the 70th week showing his final victory over the Antichrist.

results.title: The messianic count
results.text: The weeks run from the decree to the Messiah, who is cut off in the middle of the last week and confirms the new covenant; the city falls in AD 70. This is the reading this study follows.

results.title: The dispensational gap
results.text: The clock stops after the 69th week; the 70th is a future seven-year tribulation with an Antichrist treaty and a rebuilt temple.

results.title: The symbolic reading
results.text: The weeks are symbolic eras from Cyrus to the end, with the last week the church age.

results.title: The critical reading
results.text: Daniel 9 describes the Maccabean crisis, with Antiochus IV as the desolator, written about 165 BC.
